title: Where Math Breaks: The Six-Vertex Betti Flip
pitch: The paper proves Betti numbers of monomial ideals stay independent of the field's characteristic through five variables, but breaks at six — using the classic six-vertex triangulation of RP^2 (10 triangles, 15 edges, 6 vertices) as the sharp counterexample, because H_1(RP^2) has 2-torsion. Build a single self-contained HTML/JS page that hardcodes that triangulation's Stanley-Reisner ideal, computes the simplicial chain complex boundary matrices, and lets the user drag a slider between characteristic 0 (rational rank via Gaussian elimination) and characteristic 2 (rank over GF(2) via XOR row-reduction). The Betti number display visibly flips as you cross into char 2 — you literally watch a theorem's boundary case happen live. Bonus panel shows the same computation staying identical for any 5-vertex complex you draw, so users feel *why* five is safe and six isn't. Great shareable 'watch a real theorem's edge case' toy for math-Twitter/HN.

title: Bankroll Almost-Supermartingale Simulator
pitch: Olivier's classical result says a decreasing summable series a_n satisfies n*a_n -> 0; the paper extends this to 'almost supermartingales' (Robbins-Siegmund-style stochastic recursions with noise and decreasing correction terms) — exactly the shape of a bankroll or bandit-regret process with vanishing step sizes. Build a single-page canvas demo that simulates hundreds of Monte Carlo bankroll/stochastic-approximation paths X_n satisfying E[X_{n+1}|F_n] <= (1+beta_n)X_n - alpha_n + noise_n, with sliders for the decreasing sequences alpha_n, beta_n and noise variance. Plot both X_n and the rescaled n*X_n live — the punchline is watching n*X_n visibly collapse to 0 even though X_n alone looks noisy and inconclusive, and watching it fail to collapse the moment you break summability (sum beta_n = infinity). A satisfying 'see convergence rates, not just convergence' toy that speaks directly to David's poker/bankroll-math interests.

title: LLM VIX — a volatility index for production LLM APIs
pitch: The paper benchmarks how much LLM outputs vary run-to-run (same prompt, repeated queries) as a first step toward treating model volatility like a measurable financial quantity. Turn that into a running public index: continuously fire a fixed battery of prompts at GPT/Claude/Gemini/Llama endpoints, measure semantic drift (embedding cosine variance), format volatility (JSON-schema break rate), and refusal-rate variance, and publish a daily 'VIX-style' number per model plus a paid dashboard for teams that alerts them when a provider silently updates a model and output distributions shift underneath their product. Sells naturally to anyone running LLMs in a regulated or high-reliability pipeline (fits David's trading-terminal instincts — this is literally implied-vol infrastructure for the token economy).

title: Dark Proteome Explainer: small protein-LM classifier + amino-acid attribution
pitch: LA4SR shows repurposed small language models (even ~70M-1B params) can classify 'dark proteome' sequences (the ~65% of microbial/algal proteins with no known function) far faster than BLASTP, and ships an explainability layer attributing amino-acid patterns to the model's decisions. Build a scaled-down local version: fine-tune/probe a tiny protein LM (ESM2-8M or 35M, runs on a laptop) on UniProt characterized-vs-uncharacterized labels, then build an attention/gradient attribution viewer that highlights which amino-acid motifs pushed a given sequence toward 'characterized' vs 'dark', rendered as a colored sequence track. A real longer-term bio+ML project with a satisfying visual payoff (you can literally point it at a random dark protein and see which residues the model thinks matter).

title: Cutoff: The Shuffle That Suddenly Mixes
pitch: Single-file HTML deck of 52 cards (or n=1..200 slider) that runs the colored top-m-to-random shuffle live and plots total variation distance to uniform vs. shuffle count. The paper's whole point is the cutoff phenomenon: for a long stretch nothing happens (TV distance ~1), then in a razor-thin window the deck snaps to random — and with growing block size m(n) the transition even has a computable *profile* shape (not just a window), which you render as an animated erf-like curve overlaid on the live TV-distance trace. Let users drag m and n and watch the cutoff window shrink/sharpen in real time, with a poker hook: 'how many shuffles before your dealer's shuffle is actually random?' Canvas-drawn cards, no backend, pure JS math for the TV distance approximation.

title: Dispatch Oracle: Online Matching with a Cheat Sheet
pitch: A canvas game where requests (riders, or DFS lineup slots) pop up one at a time on a 2D metric and you must irrevocably match each to a server before seeing the next — classic online metric matching. Toggle a 'prediction' dial (0 = pure online / worst-case competitive ratio, 1 = omniscient offline optimum) that mirrors the paper's learning-augmented, *parsimonious* algorithm: it only consults a handful of predictions (not one per request) yet still interpolates smoothly between the two extremes. Live scoreboard shows your cost vs. the algorithm's cost vs. offline-optimal, so you feel the competitive ratio collapse as prediction quality rises. Frame it as 'draft your fantasy lineup as requests arrive' for the games angle. Single HTML file, canvas + vanilla JS, no backend.

title: Telephone Lab: Measuring Memetic Drift Across LLM Agent Chains
pitch: Build a small harness (reusing Sage's Anthropic API plumbing) that runs the children's 'telephone game' at scale: seed a message, pass it through a chain of N Claude/Haiku agents (each restating/summarizing the prior output), and measure semantic drift (embedding distance from seed) as a function of chain length and agent population size — directly testing the paper's claim that collective intelligence is a 'lottery,' i.e. multi-agent scaling laws for memetic drift can be non-monotonic and sometimes make things *worse* with more agents, not better. Sweep topology (chain vs. star vs. small-world relay), plot drift curves, and surface the regime boundary where adding agents flips from wisdom-of-crowds to garbling. Good long-running project: dashboard + nightly runs logged like your existing ideation script, publishable via the /share skill.

title: Hot Commute: Watch Mobility Create Heat Inequality
pitch: Single-file HTML city-grid simulation: draw a heat field (hotter downtown/less tree cover) and a population of dots that commute along realistic mobility patterns (home->work->home, gravity-model trip lengths). Instead of just measuring exposure by *where people live* (naive), the sim integrates exposure over each dot's actual daily path, replicating the paper's core finding that mobility patterns reshape and often worsen heat-exposure inequality versus a residence-only estimate. Slider for 'income-segregated commute distance' shows the inequality (Gini-style bar) widen as low-income dots take longer, hotter routes. Pure canvas + a small synthetic city grid, no real data needed to feel the effect, but swappable with real NYC heat/subway data later for a share.djiang.xyz post.

title: Lineup Connectome: Noise-Robust NBA Chemistry via Structural Coarse-Graining
pitch: The paper shows that computing functional connectivity on raw high-dimensional signals is noise-dominated, but first coarse-graining nodes into structurally-defined groups (before computing correlations) produces connectivity estimates that are both noise-robust AND reveal inter-subject variability that gets averaged away otherwise. Port this exact move to basketball: instead of raw player-pair on/off plus-minus correlation networks (garbage with NBA sample sizes), first coarse-grain the ~500 rotation players into structural archetype clusters (rim protector, movement shooter, initiator, etc.) via k-means on box-score profiles, THEN compute the lineup-synergy connectivity graph between archetypes across games using the paper's graph-Laplacian coarse-graining operator. This should stabilize small-sample lineup data into a real 'chemistry' signal, and per the paper's headline result, should also expose hidden team-style variability (teams whose archetype-connectivity structure diverges from their aggregate net rating) — a genuinely novel feature for the NBA props/lineup-modeling stack already in the codebase. Pulls play-by-play via nba_api, builds per-game lineup co-occurrence matrices, applies the coarse-graining transform, and validates against known lineup+/- data.

title: AgeCurve: Mixed-Effects Aging Curves as a Service
pitch: NoLimits.jl exists because pharmacometrics needs nonlinear mixed-effects models where each subject gets its own random-effect deviation from a shared nonlinear population curve — exactly the statistical shrinkage problem sports front offices and betting shops solve badly today with ad hoc, hand-fit aging/development curves per player. Build a small API (Julia backend using the same NLME machinery: population fixed effects + per-athlete random effects on a parametric curve like a logistic or Gompertz growth/decay function) that fits performance trajectories for NBA/NFL players, giving properly shrunk projections for young/small-sample players by borrowing strength from the population curve while still capturing individual deviation — directly usable for CLV-relevant player-prop pricing in the existing SharpLab/nba-modeling stack. Pitch to quant sports books and DFS shops as 'pharmacometrics-grade rigor for athlete aging curves.'

title: Random Matrix Peephole: Watch a Logical Qubit Go Chaotic
pitch: The paper's core physics move is that repeated stabilizer/syndrome projections in a surface code push the ensemble of logical states toward random-matrix-theory statistics (à la chaotic quantum-dot conductance) — eigenvalues start to REPEL each other (Wigner-Dyson spacing) instead of clustering randomly (Poisson spacing). Build a single-file HTML/JS toy: a slider labeled 'projection rounds' that morphs a live histogram of eigenvalue spacings from a small random symmetric matrix ensemble from Poisson-like (spikes near zero, eigenvalues clump) to Wigner-Dyson (the famous level-repulsion hump), with a canvas showing the actual eigenvalues as dots on a line visibly pushing apart from each other as you drag. This is the single most 'feel-it' fact in random matrix theory and almost nobody has ever seen it animate — no backend needed, just JS eigenvalue decomposition (Jacobi rotation) on small matrices, recomputed per frame.

title: TDA Shape Sculptor: Draw a Blob, See Its Persistence Diagram Live
pitch: The thymus paper's 'topological shape transform' turns organ morphology (lobulation, holes, disconnected pieces) into a persistence diagram that a classifier can use — but persistent homology is one of the most powerful and least-felt ideas in applied math. Build a single-file HTML canvas toy: freehand-draw a blob (or drag pre-set shapes with pinches/holes/multiple lobes), the page runs a live sublevel-set filtration (distance-transform threshold sweep) over a coarse pixel grid, tracks connected components and loops via union-find + a simple loop-detection pass, and renders a live-updating persistence diagram (birth/death scatter) plus barcode next to the drawing. As the user pinches a blob into two lobes or pokes a hole in it, they watch a new point appear in the persistence diagram in real time — turning an abstract algebraic-topology construction into a toy you can physically feel by drawing. No backend, pure canvas + JS, buildable in an evening.

title: Ground Truth Gate — externally-grounded verification for agent loops
pitch: A drop-in wrapper for long-running Claude Code / cron agents (starting with this very repo's nightly ideation run, plus any weekly-audit or Sentinel-style loops) that replaces self-verdict gating with an isolated 'world-state oracle' check — did tests actually pass, did the diff actually apply, did the metric actually move — instead of trusting the agent's own progress narration. The paper found self-verdict loops claim improvement every single cycle while 56% of cycles have zero-or-negative real delta, eroding best-deployed-state by 19%, and even a strong in-band judge reading the full diff still accepts 44% of regressions; a sign-only external gate recovers near-baseline real output (110 vs 113). Build it as a small Python decorator/hook that snapshots measurable world-state before/after each agent cycle and only commits when the external delta is positive, logging claimed-vs-real progress divergence so you can literally see your own agents' mirage rate over time.

title: Progress Mirage Simulator
pitch: Single-file HTML/JS toy: a fake autonomous agent grinds through 54 cycles nudging a hidden 'real-world health' score with noise. Toggle the evaluator between Self-Verdict (an LLM-flavored narrator that finds plausible-sounding progress every cycle, no matter what) and External Oracle (a grounded meter that only reports the true delta). Two racing line charts — Claimed Progress vs Real-World Delta — dramatize the paper's core numbers live: the self-verdict line climbs smoothly while the real line zeroes out or dips 56% of the time, eroding the best state by ~19%; flip to oracle mode and watch the gate reject regressions and hold the line flat-to-positive instead. Makes an abstract agent-safety failure mode viscerally felt in under a minute of play.

title: Zealots, Gridlock & Spillover
pitch: Canvas-based cellular automaton of the paper's two-party public-goods game: a grid of regions each populated by a mix of Consensus-makers, Gridlockers, and two flavors of Zealots, evolving via imitation (strategy copying from successful neighbors) plus migration toward regions with higher social+economic utility. Sliders control spillover strength and migration rate. Watch the paper's bistability emerge live — regions snap into either a permanently gridlocked stalemate or a consensus/zealot funding equilibrium — and watch poorer regions form spatial free-rider belts that calcify next to well-funded neighbors, mooching off the spillover without contributing. A striking, playable illustration of how local political dynamics harden into geography.

title: Powersort Buffer Watch
pitch: A three-way animated sorting race: classic Timsort, standard Powersort, and Virtual-Memory Powersort all sort the same shuffled array of bars, each paired with a live memory gauge showing current merge-buffer size. Timsort's gauge balloons toward n/2 elements; Virtual-Memory Powersort's barely twitches, staying near O(sqrt(n log n)) — using the exact same number of comparisons and moves (matching the paper's claim of only an additive O(n) overhead) while using almost no extra memory. A single glance explains why this near-in-place variant of the merge policy CPython adopted (Powersort) matters for sorting huge arrays.

title: Survive the Dust: an Invariance-Entropy Escape Game
pitch: Single-file HTML/canvas toy built on the paper's core object: a controlled doubling map x_{n+1} = 2x_n + u_n mod 1 that has to stay forever inside a Cantor 'dust' invariant set K (draw it as the middle-thirds set, or let the user carve their own gaps). The player controls the system through a rate-limited channel — a slider sets bits-per-step R that the 'controller' is allowed to know about the current state before picking u_n. Below the invariance entropy h_inv(K) (computable from K's gap structure/topological entropy), no strategy can keep the trajectory out of the gaps forever — you watch it eventually fall in, no matter how cleverly you play. Above it, a simple quantized feedback law survives indefinitely. It's a phase transition you can literally feel by dragging a slider, and it reframes David's poker/blind-structure interests directly: h_inv is 'the minimum bits per hand you must extract from your position to survive an escalating structure,' with the same dust/gaps as busted stacks.

title: I Simulated 10,000 Quantum Trajectories Until They Forgot Each Other
pitch: A visual explainer of propagation of chaos for Belavkin equations (continuous quantum measurement / filtering) using the classical McKean-Vlasov intuition as a bridge: N interacting noisy particles (quantum trajectories under measurement backaction) start correlated through a mean-field coupling, and as N grows the paper shows they become asymptotically independent, each obeying its own decoupled Belavkin SDE. Render this as a live particle-swarm animation (colored dots whose 'belief state' about a hidden variable decorrelates as swarm size grows) alongside a running correlation-coefficient plot crashing to zero — the payoff moment is genuinely visual. Whimsy hook for the outro: same math as why a poker table's players' updated beliefs about a shared hidden card become statistically independent draws as the table gets big — propagation of chaos as 'why crowds stop reading each other's minds.'

title: MarketDust: adaptive-agent stress lab for SharpLab's odds feeds
pitch: Build an agent-based market simulator directly feeding SharpLab: zero-intelligence + reinforcement-learning-adaptive trader agents post/take NBA prop lines, and you inject controlled 'data quality' degradation (stale ticks, dropped updates, quantization) exactly as the paper studies, then measure how CLV-capturing opportunities and mispricings emerge as a function of feed latency/quality rather than just agent sophistication. This turns a research question ('does bad data quality look like alpha, or is it actually alpha?') into a backtestable harness that validates whether SharpLab's edge-detection logic is finding real signal or exploiting book data-quality artifacts — genuinely useful before deploying more capital.

title: PatchLens: a trust score for every line an AI agent writes
pitch: The paper mined 53.6K real developer edits to AI-generated code to characterize what humans actually fix. Productize that as PatchLens: a GitHub Action / pre-commit hook that ingests your own repo history of AI-authored commits (Claude Code, Copilot, etc.) versus the diffs humans applied before merge, trains a lightweight per-line 'likely to be edited' classifier, and surfaces a confidence/trust heatmap on every new AI-generated PR before it lands — flagging the exact spans (off-by-one boundaries, error handling, naming) that this population of real edits shows get touched most. Dogfoodable immediately across David's own ~/code repos (sage, sentinel, stavid, scibowl-org) which already generate a rich AI-edit corpus, then sellable to any eng org scaling up agentic coding.

title: Patient Zero: Find the Root of a Random Recursive Tree
pitch: Single HTML-canvas toy that grows a random recursive tree node-by-node (each new node attaches uniformly to an existing one, mimicking a rumor spreading or a citation cascade), then hides the arrival order and hands you only the bare tree shape. You click to guess which node was 'born' first; then it reveals the answer via the paper's actual method — iterated Jordan centrality (repeatedly find the node minimizing max-eccentricity, peel it off, repeat) — heat-mapping every node red-to-blue by estimated arrival rank, and scores the algorithm vs. your gut guess vs. ground truth with a Spearman/Kendall-tau readout. Directly demonstrates the paper's pointwise history-estimation result: that tree topology alone leaks a surprising amount about growth order, which is exactly the epidemic-patient-zero / rumor-origin / 'who started the group chat' problem. All of it — tree generation, BFS eccentricity, iterative centrality peeling, radial layout — is trivial JS with no backend; a CDN d3 script (or hand-rolled canvas layout) is enough for one self-contained file.

title: Signature Sketchpad: Draw a Path, Watch Its Levy Area Compute Itself
pitch: A canvas where you draw (or generate a Brownian) 2D path with your mouse, and the page live-computes and visualizes its first few path-signature levels: level 1 = net displacement, level 2 = the iterated integral matrix whose antisymmetric part is the Levy area (literally the swept area between your squiggle and its chord). A side panel shows the paper's affine-structure punchline concretely: for many independent Brownian samples, the running average of the level-2 signature converges to a fixed affine/exponential relation in time (the classic 'expected signature solves the heat equation' fact) — so you watch noisy per-path signatures scatter while their average snaps onto the theoretical affine curve as you crank up the sample count. Makes an abstract rough-path-theory result (used for time-series ML and signature-based trading strategies) viscerally 'feel' like a law of large numbers you can draw with your hand. Pure canvas + trapezoidal numerical integration, no dependencies, one file.

title: Milestoning Momentum: Testing NBA 'Hot Hand' as Kinetic Hysteresis
pitch: The milestoning paper builds a rigorous framework for coarse-grained Markov-jump dynamics between 'milestones' (interfaces in state space) and shows how to detect kinetic hysteresis and fluctuation-symmetry violations when a system is driven — i.e., whether the jump rates depend on the *direction* you're moving through state space, not just the current state. Recast an NBA game's score-differential as the state space, discretize into milestone bins (e.g. every 3 points), and build the milestoning Markov-jump model from real play-by-play data (score margin trajectory per possession). Then apply the paper's thermodynamic-consistency and hysteresis-loop machinery to test a real, falsifiable question in the nba-props-terminal spirit: does the probability of the next scoring event depend on whether the margin is currently widening vs. narrowing (genuine momentum/path-dependence), beyond what a memoryless Markov null model predicts? A positive hysteresis loop would be actual statistical-physics evidence for 'momentum' as a physical effect rather than a cognitive bias narrative — a legitimately novel edge signal for the props terminal.

title: The Tree Detective: Reconstructing History From a Single Snapshot
pitch: A video essay built around the 'Patient Zero' demo: start with real hooks (finding COVID-19's patient zero, tracing a viral tweet back to its first poster, rooting a phylogenetic tree without a fossil record) and show that all of these are secretly the same math problem — given a tree's shape alone, estimate its growth order. Walk through why the Jordan center (the node minimizing worst-case distance to everyone else) tends to sit near the root of a random recursive tree, why iterating that peeling process gives a full pointwise ranking rather than just one guess, and let viewers play the on-screen demo live to beat (or lose to) the algorithm. Ends on the punchline that topology is a fossil record: shape alone remembers who came first.
